purpose: Integrate ALL current icons into the downstream application

icons.title: categorical: about all of them (כולל)
comparative: just as this, so too that (מדמה)
compound-needless: this, and needless to say that (זו ואין צריך לומר זו)
compound-not-only: not only this, but even that (לא זו אף זו)
compound: several things said together (מרבה הענינים)
conditional: an underlying assertion with a restriction or stipulation; assess both components (מגבל)
consequent: the antecedent, consequent and their dependence are all asserted, as stated (נמשך)
discrepancy: holds, even though it looks like it should not (מכחיש)
disjunction: one or the other (או... או)
exception: all of it, except this piece (מוציא)
exclusion: this and nothing else (ממעט)
hypothetical: if this, then that; only the link is claimed (תלוי)
partial: about some of them (קצתי)
particular: about this one (פרטי)
party-group: several people debating
party-individual: one person arguing both sides with himself
party-talmud: the Talmud itself, asking and answering
preclusive: not this, but rather that (לא... אלא)
qualified-certain: said as certain or necessary (ודאות / הכרח)
qualified-doubtful: said as doubtful (ספק)
qualified-impossible: said as impossible (אי אפשר)
qualified-possible: said as possible (אפשר)
simple: plainly says something about something: the statement shape itself (סתם)
unqualified: about all of them, though 'all' is not said (סתמי)
Ascribed difficulty: a problem attributed to another view
icons.description: Chapter 10, English pp214–218 and Hebrew pp213–217: a quoted document carries the existing orange Difficulty triangle. The speaker reports or reconstructs a problem for another thinker and need not endorse it. Attribution and the strength of the difficulty are separate questions.

icons.title: Ascribed proof: a report used as evidence
icons.description: Chapter 10, English p214 and Hebrew p213: reported information and demonstration operate together. A quoted document carries the existing green Proof thumb. The report and its evidential force must be evaluated separately. This does not merely mean quoting someone else’s proof.

icons.title: Priority in rank / שכלי
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p235, English p236. Intellectual or conceptual priority is precedence in rank, not chronological precedence. A crowned unit occupies the higher of two levels. The crown recalls Ramchal’s own king-and-people example; the concept is not limited to kings, intelligence, or literal physical elevation.

icons.title: Priority by dependence / טבעי
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p235, English p236. Natural priority belongs to the cause on which an effect’s existence depends, even when both exist together. A suspended block depends on its supporting beam. The support and dependent object are shown together, without a temporal arrow. The suspension is an icon metaphor, not an example quoted from Ramchal.

icons.title: Temporal priority / זמני
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p235, English p236. One thing precedes another in time. A clock accompanies two equal units in a directional sequence. The clock reading is illustrative. This is a relation of temporal precedence, separate from the Time subject badge and the Different Times statement badge.

icons.title: Attribute: preceding or following the subject
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p231, English p232. A central subject square has a companion marker before and after. A sequencing arrow represents the temporal example given here. Either relation may apply; both are not required. Ramchal later distinguishes temporal, intellectual and natural priority, so the drawing does not define all priority as time.

icons.title: Attribute: present alongside the subject
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p231, English p232. A square and separate diamond share a baseline bracket. They are present together at one time. Neither physical attachment nor causation is asserted.

icons.title: Attribute: in, on, or attached
icons.description: Three diamonds of identical size appear inside the subject square, resting on its top edge, and touching its side. These represent alternative cases, not a requirement that all occur together.

icons.title: Essence and definition: what makes the subject what it is
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p222, Hebrew p221. A single whole is precisely framed. The frame is a mnemonic for a definition that captures essential identity, not for physical shape, an inner material core, or individual identification. Essence is the thing’s what-it-is; definition states it.

icons.title: Kind and species: relative levels of inclusion
icons.description: Chapter 11, English pp228–230, Hebrew pp227–229. Nested groups show progressively narrower classifications. A classification can be a species relative to a broader kind and a kind relative to narrower species. The nesting represents classification, not component parts or a syllogistic inference.

icons.title: Perceptible form: the shape seen by the eye
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p226, Hebrew p225. The unpatterned contour of the same block used for Material focuses on visible shape. This is only the perceptible branch of Form. Essential Form is identified with essence in the text and now has its own nested-square icon at the user’s request.

icons.title: Action: the subject acts upon something else
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p226, Hebrew p225. An arrow leads from the larger subject block toward another thing. Ramchal distinguishes natural action from action chosen by a human agent. The arrow marks acting on another, not merely movement, logical entailment, or the subject’s capacity to act.

icons.title: Attribute: what accompanies a subject beyond its essence
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p231, English p232. A magnifying glass examines a square with a diamond attached at its upper-left corner. This is the parent badge for three forms of association, including concurrent and preceding/following cases; the composite is a mnemonic for examining an additional property or condition and does not imply physical contact in every case.

icons.title: Subject / נושא
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p21, English p22; also Chapter 11 distinction 21, Hebrew p233, English p234. The subject is that of which something is affirmed or denied, or the bearer sought for a given attribute. Following the user’s paired-role revision, the statement tile’s back subject cell is enlarged and emphasized, with its circle term glyph. The smaller front predicate cell and square are partially transparent. The arrow still points from subject toward predicate; it is not reversed. Emphasis identifies the subject, not amount, scope, truth, certainty, or temporal priority. The arrow is the inherited predicate carrier, not an inference or causal process. This replaces the former baseline-and-shapes Subject drawing while preserving its key.

icons.title: Being affected: an effect received from another thing
icons.description: Chapter 11, English pp226–228, Hebrew pp225–227. The arrow points from another thing toward the same larger subject block. The subject is considered as receiving an effect. The translation’s Affection does not mean fondness; receiving an effect need not involve damage.

icons.title: Cause: what brings the effect into being
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p230, Hebrew p229. A producing mechanism directs an arrow outward. The gear is a mnemonic for bringing about an effect, including both generative and effective causes, not a restriction to mechanical causes. The two causal types retain explicit text labels.

icons.title: Difference / הבדל
icons.description: Chapter 11 distinction 23. A circle and a square have different outlines, showing absence of likeness in the respect being examined. They are not mutually negating statements; there is no collision arrow or rejection mark.

icons.title: Material: what the subject is made from
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p226, Hebrew p225. A tinted block has a hatched cut surface to suggest substance. Material is what the object is made from, such as metal or clay, rather than its component parts, its shape, or the agent that makes it. The block is a mnemonic, not a claim that all material is solid.

icons.title: Means: that through which a cause acts
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p230, Hebrew p229. A wrench depicts an instrument through which an agent or cause works. Means are not restricted to hand tools; Ramchal gives a substance used to effect an action as an example.

icons.title: Motive: what prompts a voluntary agent to act
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p230, Hebrew p229. A ringing bell represents an arousing prompt. The prompt need not be a sound; the source example is news that moves Yitro to come. Motive prompts the agent, while Purpose names the end sought.

icons.title: Movement
icons.description: The same square appears at two separated positions, with an arrowed route from the lower starting position toward the upper destination. Short local ground marks emphasize a change of place.

icons.title: Opposition / נגוד
icons.description: Chapter 11 distinction 24. Two inward-facing arrowheads express opposition. This general relational badge does not select a Chapter 4 subtype and is distinct from the Chapter 9 rebuttal move דחיה. Ramchal refers back to Chapter 4 for its varieties.

icons.title: Orientation / posture
icons.description: A standing body and a seated body share one ground line. Their different configurations make posture concrete without arrows that would imply movement to another place.

icons.title: Parts: the constituents of a subject
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p222, Hebrew p221. A whole is separated into constituent pieces. The three pictured pieces are illustrative; the subject need not have three parts. Parts are not the same as the material from which a subject is made or species within a kind.

icons.title: Place: where the subject is
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p233, English p234. A location pin marks where the subject is. The source also includes relative location, such as above, beside and inside, not only map coordinates.

icons.title: Purpose: the end an agent intends to achieve
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p230, Hebrew p229. A goal flag represents the end sought through an action. It does not assert that the goal was attained. The desired end and the actual result can differ.

icons.title: Quality: the subject’s characteristics or condition
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p224, Hebrew p223. A thermometer and texture swatch suggest characteristics such as hot or cold, hard or soft, appearance, strength or weakness. Quality here does not mean excellence, a star rating, or a measured amount.

icons.title: Quantity: measurement or number
icons.description: Chapter 11, English pp224–226, Hebrew p223. A graduated ruler and three separate units represent the two cases: measuring what is measurable and counting what is countable. This differs from whether a statement applies to all, some, or one subject.

icons.title: Relation / יחס
icons.description: Chapter 11 distinction 20. Two linked chain segments symbolize one subject’s relation to another. The relation need not be physical attachment, kinship alone, similarity, or causation.

icons.title: Result: the effect that comes from a cause
icons.description: Chapter 11, English p232, Hebrew p231. An arrow emerges from a vertical dotted boundary at the far left and leads to a produced object. The cube stands for an effect, which can also be an event, motion, or living offspring. This is what follows from the cause, not necessarily what an agent intended or merely a changed recipient.

icons.title: Similarity / דמיון
icons.description: Chapter 11 distinction 22. Two overlapping circles have a shared lens, suggesting likeness in a relevant respect. The drawing does not assert complete identity, equality in every respect, or an inference from one case to another.

icons.title: Time: when the subject or event is considered
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p233, English p234. A clock represents when, including a time of day or a starting time. The illustrated clock reading is arbitrary and is not a ruling about any religious practice.

icons.title: a-fortiori: Infer from lesser to greater or greater to lesser, as the relevant predicate and comparison warrant (קל וחמר).
absolute-opposite: some do, therefore some do not: the implied box half present, half faded (הפך)
analogism: found in this one, so also in that similar one (בנין אב / מה מצינו)
classical-syllogism: Derive through an included subject or a necessary predicate connection (הקש מופתי).
contradictory: all say is, some say is not, tip to tip (מתנגדים)
contrapositive: trade places, and is becomes is not: the return arrow in negative (חלוף הפכי)
converse-limited: trade places, but it only comes back for some: a shorter, thinner return (חלוף קצתי)
converse: subject and predicate trade places: the arrow comes back the other way (חלוף כולל)
diametrically-opposed: same terms, yes against no, tip to tip (הפכיים ממש)
differs-in-context: not opposed: they speak of different settings
Different places: the statements refer to different locations
icons.description: Chapter 4: two map pins distinguish statements about different places. Chapter 11 Place retains a single map pin.

icons.title: Different times: the statements refer to different times
icons.description: Chapter 4: two separate clocks showing nine and three distinguish statements about different times. These clock readings are illustrative. The Chapter 11 Time icon remains unchanged.

icons.title: disjunctive-syllogism: Exclude all but one of an exhaustive set of alternatives, then establish the survivor (הקש מחלק).
equivalent: the same statement, twice (דומים)
fallacy-counterexample: another case just as similar lacks it
fallacy-not-greater: which case is the heavier one is not settled
fallacy-not-included: The claimed subject inclusion or necessary predicate connection fails.
fallacy-not-similar: the two cases are not alike after all (מה ל... שכן...)
figurative: not meant literally: read the allusion
has-middle: optional, praiseworthy, obligatory: a middle exists
homonym: not opposed: one word, two meanings
hypothetical-syllogism-tollens: Given an established dependency, deny the consequent and exclude the antecedent (הקש תלוי).
hypothetical-syllogism: Given an established dependency, affirm the antecedent and derive the consequent (הקש תלוי).
incongruent: different subject, different predicate (נבדלים)
inference-loose: the wording suggests it, but the line wobbles: the link is there but not firm (בלתי מוכרח)
inference-necessary: stated on the left, implied on the right (dashed: nobody said it), wired straight through (מוכרח)
no-middle: clean or unclean: nothing in between
Obverse relation / מתהפכים: corresponding subjects and predicates are opposite; assess implications separately
icons.metadata_change: Accessible title clarified only. Geometry is identical to the selected source SVG.

icons.title: statement-tile: one statement: a subject cell, a seam that says is, a predicate cell
syllogism: premises added up give a conclusion (הקש)
variant-subjects: same predicate, different subjects: two boxes, one arrow out (מתחלפים)
variant: same subject, different predicates: one box, two arrows out (מתחלפים)
actual: said of what actually does (בפועל)
dilemma: whichever way you take it, it fails (ממה נפשך)
ground-axiom: the mind dictates it, no training needed (מושכלות ראשונים)
ground-common-sense: what most people hold by nature (מפורסמות)
ground-deduction: it follows from a true premise by a deduction (הקש); the chapter 7 badge says which
ground-does-not-reach: the ground is real but does not reach the statement
ground-sense: the senses testify to it (מוחשות)
ground-tradition: handed down: a verse, a halacha, an undisputed authority (מקובלות)
might-have-thought: one might have thought otherwise; the statement is there to exclude that (סלקא דעתין / מהו דתימא)
misordered: wrong order: what should be joined is split, or the parts are out of sequence (תנא היכא קאי / ליערבינהו וליתנינהו / פתח בכד וסיים בחבית)
obvious: the whole statement adds nothing; everyone knew it (פשיטא)
potential: said of what can, not of what does: eligible, able (בכח)
rebuttal-just-the-opposite: the difficulty is thrown back at the dissenting view (אדרבא)
rebuttal-proves-my-point: your disproof text proves my view (משם ראיה / היא הנותנת)
rebuttal-your-reasoning: the same difficulty hits your view too, forcing a distinction that saves both (ולטעמיך)
redundant-part: a part of the statement repeats another (הא תו למה לי)
self-contradictory: the statement's own words disagree with each other (הא גופא קשיא)
theory: a theory inclines the mind, it does not prove (סברא)
via-opposite: the opposite is false, so this is true; or the opposite is proved, so this is false (הפך)
answer — answers it
contradiction — knocks it down
difficulty — raises a problem
proof — backs it up
question — someone asks
resolution — clears the problem
statement — someone speaks
Alternative: lightbulb with a dotted bridge and open center
icons.description: The equally bright Resolution bulb contains a dotted bridge-like filament and an open circle. They mark a viable interpretation offered to remove a difficulty without committing to it as the actual explanation. The dotted route is provisional, not a broken or invalid defense.

icons.title: Apparent contradiction: two opposing chevrons inside a warning triangle
icons.description: Two equally weighted shapes press toward each other inside the Difficulty triangle. Both sides remain present; their apparent conflict calls for reconciliation.

icons.title: Demonstration: monitor with thumbs up
icons.description: A demonstration is represented by a monitor containing the Proof family’s thumbs-up symbol. The move seeks to establish a statement; the icon does not certify the argument.

icons.title: Objection: incoming impact inside a warning triangle
icons.description: A projectile is directed at an upright statement block: an objection is thrown at the original speaker’s statement. The statement remains standing; the picture does not assert its defeat.

icons.title: Opposition: crossed circle with branching arrows
icons.description: The red crossed circle identifies the Contradiction family; two outgoing arrows distinguish Opposition, which removes certainty while leaving the statement possible.

icons.title: Settlement: lightbulb with a continuous bridge and check
icons.description: The shared bulb identifies Resolution. A continuous bridge-like filament and check depict an explanation the proposer endorses as true. This marks the offered kind of resolution, not an independent verdict that it is correct; its two terminals do not require two source statements.

icons.title: Validation: two facing thumbs up
icons.description: Two thumbs face each other to represent one statement agreeing with and supporting another. Validation is a subtype of Proof.

icons.title: Stated teaching / שמועה
icons.description: A tall speech bubble with three statement lines fills the document interior. The speech tail remains distinct.

icons.title: Explanation / פרוש
icons.description: Selected wording at the top connects through a longer annotation leader to a two-line gloss below. The leader has no arrowhead.

icons.title: Inference / דיוק
icons.description: Three lines of source text are grouped above a rule. A centered arrow descends to a separate point below, representing what was not explicitly stated.

icons.title: Reported information / הגדה
icons.description: An enlarged upper speech bubble contains the person being reported about. A second, larger reporter sits beneath the bubble, toward its tail. The report can concern deeds, words, or thoughts.

icons.title: Order / סדר
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p237, English p238. Units are neatly aligned in two rows. Order assists both learning and teaching through Arrangement, Definitions, and Division. The drawing expresses organization, not a fixed number of topics, a deduction, a chronology, or a fourth principle.

icons.title: Arrangement / סדור
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew pp237–241, English pp238–242. A play-diagram motif routes three items along distinct paths to their intended positions. Present what must be understood first before what depends on it, proceeding from the more known to the less known. Ramchal includes general before particular and simple before composite. This is order of exposition, not an assertion that the subject matter happens in this sequence.

icons.title: Definitions / גדרים
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p241, English p242. A plain bulleted list represents the defining features stated explicitly. Definitions should include the whole essential content without substituting incidental properties. The three pictured entries are illustrative, not a required number of features. No arrow or sequence is asserted.

icons.title: Division / analysis / חלוק
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew pp241–245, English pp242–246. One bounded whole is partitioned into two regions, then smaller subregions. The regions together cover the whole without gaps or overlaps. Deeper subdivisions remain inside their parent regions. Counts and areas are illustrative, not numerical claims. This is recursive analysis of a topic, distinct from the existing Parts badge and from a syllogistic inference tree.

icons.title: Theoretical knowledge / חכמות שכליות
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew pp237–239, English pp238–240. An orbiting heavenly body recalls Ramchal’s astronomy example: understanding a subject of reality as it is. The category includes other sciences, not astronomy alone. It does not mean tentative theory (סברא), intellectual priority, or one particular ground of evidence. The recommended exposition proceeds through subject, parts, causes, and attributes.

icons.title: Practical knowledge / חכמות מעשיות
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew pp237–241, English pp238–242. The established Purpose flag accompanies the established Means wrench. Practical knowledge teaches how to carry out an art: explain the intended end first, then the required means. Ramchal gives grammar and calendar calculation, so the category is not limited to manual crafts or physical tools. No success is asserted.

icons.title: Full explanation / פרוש מרוח
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew p163, English p164. The upper wording and lower explanatory text meet at a fitted puzzle seam inside the Statement document. Full explanation fits the statement completely. The seam marks fit, not a separate proof or truth verdict.

icons.title: Forced explanation / פרוש דחוק
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew p163, English p164. The same puzzle seam keeps the central connection intact, while the lower explanation is squeezed inward by two arrows. The essential message fits, but wording or arrangement fits poorly. This is strain in explanatory fit, not coercion of a speaker or complete rejection.

icons.title: Ukimta: specifying the case / אוקימתא
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew pp163–165, English pp164–166. Unchanged wording at the top accompanies a narrowing funnel and one bounded case below. Ukimta supplies a condition restricting the application while retaining the plain meaning of the words. The funnel restricts the case, not the wording. This is a method of explanation, not a third grade of fit or necessarily a forced reading.

icons.title: Query / שאלה
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew pp167–169, English pp168–170. The Question mark sits over one open response field. A Query requests whether a matter is so, or a circumstance such as place, time, or reason. The single field means the requested information, not a requirement of a one-word answer.

icons.title: Two-sided question / אבעיא
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew p169, English p170. The Question mark branches into two equal empty option boxes. There are grounds for two sides and the question asks which should be decided. The fork does not mean that every yes/no query is an Ibayya.

icons.title: Answer to a query / תשובת השאלה
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew p171, English p172. Supplied information sits above the same single response field, now containing the established Answer check. The answer supplies what the query asks and must be true and appropriate. The check means an answer has been supplied, not that its content must be yes or that its truth has been independently verified.

icons.title: Determination / פשיטות
icons.description: Chapter 9, Hebrew pp171–173, English pp172–174. A fork ends at two options inside the established Answer frame. One option contains a check; the other remains unselected. Determination decides one of the two sides of an Ibayya. The chosen left side is illustrative, not a source rule, and this is not פשיטא or a separate Proof or Contradiction move.

icons.title: Natural action / פעלה טבעית
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p225, English p226. The Action source block contains flowing waves; the shared outward arrow leads to another thing. The waves symbolize activity by nature, including nonliving things. They do not restrict natural action to liquids, heat, or involuntary human behavior.

icons.title: Voluntary action / פעלה רצונית
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p225, English p226. A hand deliberately activates a control inside the Action source block; the same outward arrow leads to another thing. Intentional activation is a mnemonic for human choice. It does not limit voluntary action to hands, physical controls, or bodily work.

icons.title: Generative cause / סבה מולדת
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p229, English p230. The inherited Cause gear sends out a continuous stem that branches into a smaller gear of the same family. The repeated form and uninterrupted connection indicate a continuation from its source, as in the tree and its fruit or a father and child. This does not assert identical properties, literal machinery, or permanent physical attachment.

icons.title: Effective cause / סבה פועלת
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p229, English p230. The inherited Cause gear directs an arrow toward a separate produced object, using the Result family cube. The object is produced by the cause but is not a continuation of it. The cube is a mnemonic for any effect, including an event or changed understanding, not a restriction to manufactured objects.

icons.title: Inseparable property / סגולה
icons.description: Chapter 8, Hebrew p147, English p148. A compact closed chain binds the upper-left property diamond to the lower-right subject square. The chain is approximately half the previous length, with short attachment stems. Complete diamond and square outlines remain dominant; no broad white outline covers them. Two coupled links make inseparability the relationship between the two shapes. Their separate identities show that the property accompanies the subject rather than constituting its essence. This analytical icon does not assert physical bondage, exclusivity to a species, or mystical power. It is not a declared child of Chapter 11 Attribute.

icons.title: Essential form: the defining structure within the whole
icons.description: Chapter 11, Hebrew p225, English p226. An outer square encloses four corner brackets, which frame a substantial solid inner square. Following user feedback, the inner square is twice its original width and the brackets move outward, making the center read as the defining structure of the larger whole. Ramchal explicitly identifies essential form with the subject's essence. This separate contextual icon does not assert a literal anatomical skeleton, a material component, or a philosophical distinction from essence.

icons.title: Premise / הקדמה
icons.description: Chapter 7, Hebrew p93, English p94. A solid teal statement unit starts a downward outgoing inference arrow aimed toward a dotted horizontal boundary beneath it. The dots represent the further reasoning into which this premise feeds. The filled unit is the statement taken as the starting point of this deduction; the badge does not certify independent truth. This is a logical role, not a new Chapter 9 move or a causal event.

icons.title: Conclusion / תולדה
icons.description: Chapter 7, Hebrew p93, English p94. A downward arrow emerges from a dotted horizontal boundary above it and arrives at an outlined, lightly tinted teal statement unit. The dots represent the prior reasoning from which this conclusion emerges. It marks the statement derived in this deduction. The outline denotes the derived role, not uncertainty. A conclusion is not the causal Result badge, a final verdict, or a requirement that every argument have only one premise.

icons.title: Antecedent / הקודם
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p31, English p32. The selected violet Hypothetical Statement vocabulary retains two upright outlined dominoes and its exact dependency arrow. The left clause is enlarged and emphasized to identify the condition clause; the smaller partner preserves context. Both remain outlined because the hypothetical asserts their dependence without asserting either clause has occurred. Emphasis denotes the part being identified, not truth, certainty, amount, causal force, or temporal priority. This is a part-role of a hypothetical statement, not a Chapter 9 subtype. The Consequent part is distinct from the existing whole Consequent Statement icon.

icons.title: Consequent / הנמשך
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p31, English p32. The selected violet Hypothetical Statement vocabulary retains two upright outlined dominoes and its exact dependency arrow. The right clause is enlarged and emphasized to identify the dependent clause; the smaller partner preserves context. Both remain outlined because the hypothetical asserts their dependence without asserting either clause has occurred. Emphasis denotes the part being identified, not truth, certainty, amount, causal force, or temporal priority. This is a part-role of a hypothetical statement, not a Chapter 9 subtype. The Consequent part is distinct from the existing whole Consequent Statement icon.

icons.title: Predicate / נשוא
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p21, English p22. What is affirmed or denied of a subject. The established violet statement tile is adapted to emphasize its right-hand arrow-shaped predicate cell and square term glyph. A smaller, lighter subject cell and circle preserve the relation. The arrow is the term-role carrier, not a separate inference, a causal process, or a timeline. Emphasis identifies the predicate, not truth, negation, uncertainty, scope, importance, or amount. The tile remains outlined; its solid internal glyph represents a term. This is a role within a statement, not a Chapter 9 discussion move or a kind of attribute.

icons.title: Equal-footing compound / בהשואה אחת
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p33, English p34. Two equal circles sit at the same height inside the established violet compound bracket. The predications are presented on equal footing. Equal size does not mean synonymous content, numerical equality, equal probability, or equal certainty. Two units illustrate plurality without restricting the source to exactly two. The bracket groups coasserted content; no inference is drawn. Ramchal describes this branch without assigning it a separate formal Hebrew name.

icons.title: Known-and-novel compound / בדרך חדוש · שכבר נודע
icons.description: Chapter 3, Hebrew p33, English p34. A plain circle and a four-point starburst sit at the same height inside the established violet compound bracket. One assertion is presented as already known, the other as a novel point. The starburst is a mnemonic for novelty, not greater truth, certainty, holiness, a question, or a resolution. No arrow or staircase specifies which is said first. Left/right positions are illustrative. The two source orders remain separate child icons. Ramchal describes this branch without assigning it a separate formal Hebrew name.

icons.title: Natural ground / ראיה מצד הטבע
icons.description: Chapter 8, Hebrew p111, English p112. Naturally manifest truths, or statements based on them. The established Axiom sun and Sense face share one ground as the two branches of this parent category. Either branch can ground a statement; both are not required together. Nature here concerns axiomatic intellect and sensory evidence, not ecology or natural causation.

icons.title: Conventional ground / ראיה מצד ההסכמה
icons.description: Chapter 8, Hebrew p113, English p114. A view accepted within a community, or a statement based on it. The established Common Judgments people and Tradition hands share one ground as the two branches of this parent category. Either branch can ground a statement; both are not required together. This does not mean individual intuition or a vote deciding universal truth.

icons.title: Disjunctive deduction: affirm one, exclude the others / הקש מחלק
icons.description: Chapter 7, Hebrew pp105–107, English pp106–108. Given exactly one of the alternatives, establishing one excludes all the others. The selected disjunctive fork, solid right node and crossed left branch are preserved under one uniform transform. A new arrow runs from the established right alternative to the rejected left alternative. It marks the direction of reasoning, not a temporal or causal process.
